one_liner: Nim /proc query toolkit whose pd/pf/pk read fewer /proc files than procps ps, pgrep and pkill.
what_it_does: procs is a single Nim binary and library with subcommands display (pd, a ps/top-style lister), find (pf for pgrep/pidof, pk for pkill, pw for waiting on unrelated PIDs) and scrollsy (sc, vmstat-like system stats); the short names are symlinks that select a subcommand. Output columns, colours, process 'kinds' and row merging are user-defined through config files under ~/.config/procs or an installed etc/procs, so it is a ps construction kit, not a drop-in ps. pf takes pgrep-like options, but its patterns are unanchored PCRE searches on the 15-character comm, or on the full command line with --full.
how_it_is_fast: Demand-driven /proc reads: each format code or filter declares the ProcFields it needs, and needs() maps them to the minimal set of files. A '%p %c' listing or a name match therefore opens only /proc/PID/stat, while procps also opens and parses status and, for pgrep, cmdline. It reuses one IO buffer for every readFile and parses stat in place with memory slices. pf/pk act 'ASAP' as each process matches, and --exist returns at the first match, whereas procps pgrep/pkill read and select all processes before acting.
when_to_use: Scripts or interactive use on Linux that call pgrep/pkill/pidof often, especially 'does a process named X exist' checks (pf -e), where the first-match exit and stat-only reads cut wall time by 4x or more
Killing runaway processes on an overloaded box: pk sends signals as each match is found instead of after a full scan
Custom ps/top-style reports (merged kernel threads, per-category colours, diffs every N seconds with pd -d1) where you would otherwise post-process ps output
Nim programs that want a typed /proc reader (procs is also a library) that reads only the fields asked for
when_not_to_use: Anything that is not Linux /proc: no BSD, macOS or Windows support
Scripts that rely on exact pgrep/ps semantics: pf has no -x exact mode (use '^name$'), patterns are PCRE not POSIX ERE, and pd's formats differ from ps's

Rich listings: speed comes from reading less, so formats that need status, cmdline, io or smaps lose most of the gap (the README shows pd at 1.27x over ps once its default kinds and highlights are on, and says there are configurations where ps can be faster)

Locked-down or minimal systems: it needs Nim and cligen to build, PCRE1 (libpcre, loaded by Nim's std/nre) at run time, and a config tree; the author calls it a work in progress with 'surely many bugs'

integration.form: module plus CLI binary (nimble package procs; pd, pf, pk, pw, sc are symlinks)
integration.dependencies: cligen >= 1.10.0; Nim stdlib including std/nre, which loads the PCRE1 shared library at run time; optional config files (configs/cb0)
integration.min_toolchain: Nim >= 1.6.0 per procs.nimble, built with --threads:on (procs.nims); C backend compiler version not documented
integration.platforms: Linux only (/proc); README reports Gentoo, Debian and Android Termux
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the library parses every /proc file through one global shared buffer ('var buf ... shared IO buffer for all readFile'), so do not call its readers from several threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: pf/pk take options 'most similar to pgrep' and default to SIGTERM like pkill, but matching is unanchored PCRE on comm with no -x; pd is not ps-compatible (user-defined formats and config files)

gotchas: bench.sh never times pkill, only pgrep. The README's '(5.745±0.016)X slower than pk' is the i7-1370P pgrep row divided by the mean of pf's first-hit and no-match times (derived from page data). That 'average process' figure assumes pf stops at the first match; pk, which signals every match, has to scan everything, so the equal-work ratios are 3.75x (i7-6700K) and 4.12x (i7-1370P).

In bench.sh the pf pattern is the comm of the first /proc entry ($p), but the pgrep side is hard-coded 'pgrep -x init'. On a systemd machine (PID 1 comm 'systemd') a user re-running it would compare pf's first-entry hit against pgrep's no-match scan. pf's match is also an unanchored substring, not pgrep's exact -x.

The README ps comparison is not like for like: 'pd -f%p %c' with PROCS_CONFIG=/n prints the pid and the 15-character comm from /proc/PID/stat ('%c' is pf_cmd; '%C' would be the full command line), while '/bin/ps ax' prints PID, TTY, STAT, TIME and the full argv. No equal-output run such as 'ps -eo pid=,comm=' was timed.

Config fragility: the shipped cb0 config raised 'unknown color key: "rcuS"' exceptions after an update (issue #8, fixed 2025-05-28), and 0.8.14 fixed an fd leak in pf --newest/--oldest; the tool parses its config on every run unless PROCS_CONFIG points to an empty file.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued siblings it is the only process-table tool. It shares the 'issue fewer syscalls' approach of the author's cligen/dents walker and bu tools (dups, mk1), and like hexdump-rs or neosmart tac it replaces a coreutils-era C utility. Pick it when pgrep/pkill/ps latency or ASAP signalling matters on Linux and you can live with different option semantics.
verified_claims_summary: bench.sh (added 2025-04-01; the author's tim tool, chrt 99 taskset -c 2, wrapper overhead subtracted): on an i7-6700K with about 196 processes, pf -e1 with no match took 2.06 ms vs 'pgrep -x init' at 7.72 ms (3.75x); on an i7-1370P with about 323 processes, 1.35 ms vs 5.54 ms (4.12x). Stopping at PID 1 gives the 'up to' 7.6x and 9.5x. The README footnote times 'pd -f%p %c' at 2.86 ms vs '/bin/ps ax' at 5.03 ms (1.76x, different output, machine unnamed), and 3.97 ms (1.27x) with default kinds and highlights. Nim, C compiler, flags and procps versions are unstated.
status_note: Active single-author project (last commit 2026-07-04, version 0.8.14, 25 stars, ISC LICENSE text although the nimble file says 'MIT/ISC'). A WebSearch snippet of the 1996 procps-1.01 LSM lists Charles Blake as a procps co-author (page not opened). Small enough to vendor, but it ties you to Nim, cligen, PCRE1 and its config tree, and the measured wins are millisecond-scale and depend on narrow formats.
